title: Warnings from the Wilderness and the Table of the Lord
summary: Paul warns that Israel in the wilderness had its own baptism and spiritual food, yet most of them fell through idolatry, immorality, and grumbling, and their story was written down as a warning. He tells the Corinthians to flee idolatry, because sharing in the Lord's cup and table cannot be combined with sharing in meals offered to demons. He closes the long discussion of idol food with practical guidance for the market and private dinners: do all to the glory of God and seek the good of others.
story: This chapter completes the argument that began in chapter 8. There Paul agreed that idols are nothing but urged love for the weak; in chapter 9 he gave his own example of surrendering rights. Now he addresses the strong directly: their confidence is dangerous, because sacramental privilege did not keep Israel from falling. He distinguishes two situations. Eating in a temple's cultic meal is idolatry and is forbidden outright (verses 14 to 22). Eating meat from the market or at a friend's table is free, unless someone's conscience is at stake (verses 23 to 33). The reference to the cup and the bread (verses 16 and 17) also prepares for the fuller discussion of the Lord's Supper in chapter 11.
historical:
Paul retells events from Exodus and Numbers: the cloud and the crossing of the sea (Exodus 13 and 14), manna and water from the rock (Exodus 16 and 17; Numbers 20), the golden calf and the feast that followed (Exodus 32:6, quoted in verse 7), the sin with the women of Moab at Baal Peor (Numbers 25), the bronze serpent episode (Numbers 21), and the grumbling rebellions that ended in plague (Numbers 14 and 16). The Corinthian church was largely Gentile, yet Paul calls the Israelites “our forefathers” (verse 1), treating Gentile believers as members of Israel's family through Christ.

The detail that the rock “accompanied them” (verse 4) reflects a Jewish tradition, found in later rabbinic sources and possibly already current in Paul's day, that a well or rock followed Israel through the wilderness. Water came from a rock both near the start of the wilderness period (Exodus 17) and near its end (Numbers 20), which may have encouraged the idea.
cultural:
Sacrifices in the Greek and Roman world ended in a meal. Part of the animal was burned for the god, part went to the priests, and the rest was eaten by the worshipers, often in dining rooms on the temple grounds, with the god considered the host or honored guest. Surviving papyrus invitations from Roman Egypt invite guests to dine at the table of the god Serapis, which shows how natural Paul's phrase “the table of demons” would have sounded as a contrast with “the table of the Lord” (verse 21). Israel's own sacrifices worked similarly: those who ate them shared in the altar (verse 18).

Outside the temples, meat sold at the city market (the macellum, verse 25) might or might not have come from a sacrifice, and no one could easily tell. Paul permits believers to buy it and to eat whatever is served at a private dinner without asking. His ground is Psalm 24:1, “The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof,” a verse later rabbinic teaching cited as the reason to bless God before eating.
literary: Verses 1 to 13 are a piece of typology, reading Israel's history as a pattern that foreshadows the church's situation. Paul repeats “all” five times in verses 1 to 4 (all under the cloud, all passed through the sea, all baptized, all ate, all drank) and then turns sharply: “Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them.” Four warnings follow, each marked by “as some of them did.” Verses 14 to 22 argue from the nature of sacred meals, and verses 23 to 33 return to the Corinthian slogan “Everything is permissible” and qualify it twice. The chapter ends by gathering the whole discussion into one principle (verse 31) and one example (Paul's own, 10:33 to 11:1).

outline.t: Written for us: God's faithfulness in temptation
Flee idolatry: one loaf, one body
The table of the Lord and the table of demons
The market, the dinner invitation, and conscience
Do all to the glory of God

doctrines.note: Idols themselves are nothing, but “the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons” (verse 20), echoing Deuteronomy 32:17. Idolatry is not a harmless error; it is fellowship with spiritual powers opposed to God, and it provokes the Lord to jealousy (verse 22).

The cup and the bread are a “participation” in Christ's blood and body (verse 16), and eating the one loaf makes many into one body (verse 17). Christians differ on how Christ is present in the Supper, but all traditions draw from this verse that the meal is real communion with Christ and with one another, not an empty sign.
“God is faithful” (verse 13). Temptation is common to all, but God sets its limits and provides a way to endure it. The verse promises strength to stand, not a life without testing.

words.note: Koinonia, sharing, participation, fellowship, partnership. It describes a common share in something. In verse 16 the cup and bread are a koinonia in Christ's blood and body; the same logic makes eating at a temple feast a sharing with demons (verse 20 uses the related word for participants). The word is often translated communion, which is where that name for the Lord's Supper comes from.

Tupos, a pattern, example, or type, originally the mark left by a blow or a stamp. Israel's experiences happened as “examples” (verse 6). This is the root of typology: events in Israel's history that prefigure and illuminate the church's life in Christ.

Peirasmos, testing or temptation. The same word covers trials that test faith and enticements to sin. Verse 13 promises that no peirasmos is unique and that God will provide an “escape,” a word used for a way out of a pass or a narrow place.

Petra, rock, the rock from which Israel drank. Paul says “that rock was Christ” (verse 4), identifying the pre-existent Christ as the source of Israel's life in the wilderness. The Old Testament frequently calls God the Rock of Israel (for example Deuteronomy 32).

christ: Paul makes a bold claim: “that rock was Christ” (verse 4), and Israel “tested Christ” in the wilderness (verse 9; some manuscripts read the Lord). Christ was present with Israel before his birth, sustaining his people. Paul sees in Israel's exodus a pattern of baptism and spiritual food that finds its meaning in Christ, and he places the church at the point where “the fulfillment of the ages has come” (verse 11). At the Lord's table, believers share in Christ's body and blood, the benefits of his death, and are joined into one body. Christ alone is the host of his people's meal, and he will not share his table with rival gods.

hard.q: Why does Paul say twenty-three thousand died in one day, when Numbers 25:9 says twenty-four thousand?
hard.a: Readers have noticed this since ancient times. Several explanations are offered. Some suggest Paul is referring to those who died in one day, while Numbers counts the total over the whole plague. Others think Paul is recalling a different incident, perhaps conflating the plague at Baal Peor with the aftermath of the golden calf in Exodus 32 (verse 7 has just quoted that story), though Exodus 32:28 gives about three thousand. Others simply note that Paul was quoting from memory and giving round numbers, as ancient writers commonly did, and that his point does not depend on the exact figure. The discrepancy is minor and was freely acknowledged by early Christian interpreters. What matters to Paul's argument is that a people who had seen God's power and eaten his provision still fell through immorality.

questions: Paul warns, “the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall.” Where are you most confident, and could that confidence be a danger?
The Corinthians thought their religious privileges protected them. What spiritual privileges might we be trusting instead of God?
What would it look like to do ordinary things, eating and drinking included, “to the glory of God” this week?
